t: Find Subarrays With Equal Sum — Editorial
o: We need to check whether any two length-2 subarrays (starting at different indices) have the same sum. A length-2 subarray starting at index i has sum nums[i] + nums[i+1], so the problem reduces to: do two adjacent-pair sums repeat anywhere? For [4,2,4] the pair sums are 6 and 6, so we return true; for [1,2,3,4,5] they are 3,5,7,9 — all distinct, so false. For [0,0,0] both pairs sum to 0, and since they start at different indices they count. With n up to 1000, even an O(n^2) brute force is fine, but a hash set gives a clean O(n) solution.
k: There are exactly n-1 length-2 subarrays, with sums s[i] = nums[i] + nums[i+1].
The answer is true iff any value appears twice among these n-1 sums.
A hash set lets us detect a duplicate sum in one pass, O(n) time and space.

a.i: Compute all n-1 adjacent-pair sums into an array, then compare every pair of sums with two nested loops. If any two sums are equal, return true. This directly mirrors the problem statement and needs no extra data structures beyond the sums array.
s: Build array s where s[i] = nums[i] + nums[i+1] for i in 0..n-2.
For every i < j, if s[i] == s[j], return true.
If no equal pair is found, return false.
a.t: O(n^2) — comparing all pairs of n-1 sums dominates.
a.sp: O(n) — storing all n-1 pair sums.

a.i: Instead of storing all sums and comparing later, keep a hash set of sums seen so far while scanning left to right. For each index i compute nums[i] + nums[i+1]; if it is already in the set, we found two distinct subarrays with equal sum. Otherwise insert it and continue.
s: Initialize an empty hash set seen.
For each i from 0 to n-2, compute sum = nums[i] + nums[i+1].
If sum is already in seen, return true.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average hash set operations.
a.sp: O(n) — the set can hold up to n-1 distinct sums.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly, then present the hash-set one-pass solution as the answer — it is simple, optimal, and easy to verify. Pitfalls: remember the two subarrays only need different starting indices (identical content at different positions counts, as in Example 3); use 64-bit arithmetic in C++/Java since each element can be up to 10^9 in magnitude, making pair sums up to 2*10^9 which overflows 32-bit ints. Edge cases: minimum-length arrays like [x, y] always return false; arrays with many zeros or repeated patterns return true quickly. Follow-ups might ask you to return the actual indices of the matching subarrays (store sum -> first index in a map), or generalize to subarrays of length k (slide a window and hash window sums).
